one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the 30th anniversary of Edsa 1 (Feb 22-25, 1986) and the 15th of Edsa 2 (Jan 16-20, 2001, recently passed without fanfare) by drawing both parallels and contrasts. Both revolutions were confluences of unplanned events joined by the middle class and the masses (the 'perfumed' and 'unperfumed' to one pundit, 'bourgeois' and 'proletariat' to an ideologue), happening at the corner of Edsa and Ortigas with the active support of the Church (personified by Cardinal Sin) and the military -- without which neither revolution would have ousted its president or installed Cory and Arroyo respectively. From the legal view, however, the similarity ends there. Edsa 1 was extra-constitutional -- undertaken against the then-prevailing 1973 Constitution under which Marcos had been proclaimed snap-election winner. Cory issued Proclamation 1 announcing she and VP Laurel were taking power, then Proclamation 3 stating that the 'new government was installed through a direct exercise of the power of the Filipino people assisted by units of the New Armed Forces of the Philippines.' She did not ascend via the snap election or the 1973 Constitution. The Cory-era Supreme Court -- composed of her appointees -- summarily concluded in Lawyers League vs Aquino (May 22, 1986) that the legitimacy of her government was not a 'justiciable' controversy; nonetheless, popular acceptance and international recognition made it a de jure government. By contrast, in Estrada vs Desierto (March 2, 2001), an SC with mostly non-Cory appointees affirmed the legitimacy of her ascent -- and rejected Arroyo's lawyers' attempt to invoke the same 'political thicket' defense. The Court held that political questions relate to matters of 'wisdom, not the legality,' delegated by the people to the executive or legislative branch; the 1987 Constitution, unlike its forebears, had trimmed the political thicket by giving the judiciary expanded duties: determining grave abuse of discretion by any branch of government, and reviewing the factual basis of martial law or habeas corpus suspension. The Court distinguished Edsa 1 as 'an exercise of the people power of revolution which overthrew the whole government' from Edsa 2 as 'an exercise of people power of freedom of speech and freedom of assembly to petition the government for redress of grievances which only affected the office of the President' -- Edsa 1 extra-constitutional, Edsa 2 intra-constitutional and subject to judicial review. In other words, Edsa 1 obliterated the 1973 Constitution and all the government institutions under it (including the SC itself), which is why its legitimacy was repeatedly challenged through coup attempts until the people ratified the 1987 Constitution; Edsa 2 preserved the 1987 Charter and its institutions. This is why Estrada vs Desierto explained Edsa 2's constitutionality at length while Lawyers League vs Aquino is notable for its sheer brevity. Sadly for Arroyo, her public satisfaction plunged after her 2004 electoral victory was severely questioned and her governance vilified as corrupt and ineffective. In both revolutions the Church played a pivotal role -- and a 'little-known but serious internal conflict, involving Cardinal Sin and the Vatican, nearly blurred that role,' which Panganiban promises to write about at another time (the column that becomes C89).
